source.title: Banishing LLM Hallucinations Requires Rethinking Generalization
source.authors: John Li; Saksham Consul; Eda Zhou; J. Wong; N. Farooqui; Yuxin Ye; Nithyashree Manohar; Zhuxiaona Wei; Tian Wu; Benjamin Echols; Sharon Zhou; G. Diamos

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Tests random-label fitting and generalization in pretrained LLMs using a different setup from the original image-classification experiments.
record.gate_note: Rows cover random-answer fine-tuning and reported generalization on unrelated questions. The paper reports Llama 3 and MoME loss curves as figures without extracted numerical values. Table 1 gives individual examples, not aggregate test-error rates. It does not test unstructured image inputs, corrupted-label fractions, regularization removal, or learning real patterns before noisy ones. Claims about MMLU and precise recall in the Insights section lack corresponding numerical results here.
record.test_reason: The study extends random-label fitting tests to pretrained language models. Its own experiments report near-zero training loss on randomized answers and compare training on real versus random answers.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that pretrained LLMs can memorize random answers while retaining performance on unrelated questions, that generalization error does not discriminate hallucination behavior, and that precise memorization requires substantial additional computation. They propose MoME to reduce that computation. Their generalization claims exceed the aggregate numerical evidence supplied here.
record.recipe_differences: Pretrained language models are fine-tuned on question-answer data with random character strings, rather than training image classifiers from scratch on randomly labeled images; Llama 3 uses frozen backbone weights and LoRA adapters with Adafactor.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported tests vary model architecture (Llama 3, Mistral v2, MoME), dataset (TruthfulQA, MMLU), and answer condition (true versus random). Outcome values are not separately reported for each combination.

fits_no_version.finding: Answers to unrelated factual questions remain mostly unchanged after random-answer fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretrained language models can retain unrelated factual capabilities while memorizing randomized answers.

fits_no_version.finding: MoME reaches near-zero real-answer and random-answer training loss after 100 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A pretrained language model augmented with selectively trained memory experts can memorize randomized answers.

record.problems: Training-loss findings are shown in figures without numeric values or uncertainty; generalization is characterized as mostly unchanged without a numerical aggregate test-error measure. Table 1 provides only a few illustrative examples. The text does not report model-by-dataset outcome breakdowns.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. The approximately 100-epoch and approximately 100x-more-SGD-steps statements are not entered as separate rows because they are not a directly compared measured timing result; the text does not test convergence as corrupted-label fraction varies.

untested.parts: Chance test error on held-out random targets; numerical training-error rates; fitting with an unmodified, fully trained standard network. The detailed experiment freezes a pretrained backbone and trains LoRA adapters; unchanged hyperparameters across answer conditions are not explicitly documented.
A measured wall-clock training-time ratio and convergence as the fraction of corrupted labels increases.
A corruption-fraction sweep measuring training fit and test error.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and removing these regularizers.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels within training.

record.verdict_notes: The approximately 100-fold step increase compares precise memorization with the usual single-epoch training recipe, not random labels with true labels; it therefore does not challenge V2. Unrelated-question retention does not challenge V1's chance-error clause. Figure curves are not visible in the supplied text, so conclusions about them rely on captions and the authors' descriptions.

versions.untested_parts: Original standard deep networks on image datasets; exact zero training error and chance test error; unchanged architecture and optimizer hyperparameters. This study uses pretrained LLMs, random-answer fine-tuning, and unrelated-question evaluations.

The text states approximately 100 epochs and approximately 100x more SGD steps than usual, but does not give a directly comparable measured training-time ratio or a sweep over fractions of corrupted labels.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from no corrupted labels to all corrupted labels, with measured perfect training fit and steady test-error increase.
The study does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation against random labels, or their removal on true-label generalization.
The study does not compare learning trajectories of real patterns versus noisy labels to establish which are learned first.

rows.subject: Llama 3 8B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on question-answer data with answers replaced by random 32-bit strings; backbone frozen and LoRA adapters tuned.
rows.baseline: True-answer fine-tuning; separate value not stated
rows.note: The paper describes the curves and result in text; no precise curve values are stated.
rows.check: Figure 1 compares real-answer and random-answer training; both reach near-zero loss after 100 epochs, and Section 2 describes their loss curves as mostly unaffected by randomization. Replace the unspecified baseline with this qualitative comparison. The main text describes 32 random characters, whereas Appendix A inconsistently describes 32-bit strings. Near-zero loss is reported, without a numerical training-error rate.

rows.subject: Mistral v2
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on question-answer data with answers replaced by random characters.
rows.measure: Ability to fit random-answer training data
rows.value: The paper states pre-trained LLMs achieve zero finetuning error; model-specific result not stated
rows.note: The results are described collectively for standard architectures including Llama 3 and Mistral v2; no model-specific error value is given.
rows.check: The authors explicitly include Mistral v2 in their collective zero-finetuning-error finding. Missing model-specific numbers do not establish a partial effect. Retain the collective attribution and flag the absence of a separate Mistral result.

rows.subject: Llama 3
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated answers to unrelated held-out questions after random-answer fine-tuning.

conditions.value: unrelated questions; TruthfulQA test set and MMLU

rows.note: The text describes performance collectively; no numerical aggregate or separate model-specific measure is stated.
rows.check: Accuracy on unrelated factual questions measures retention of pretrained capabilities. It does not measure chance-level prediction of held-out random labels or incomplete random-label fitting. The text reports this collectively rather than as a separate Llama 3 aggregate result.

rows.subject: Llama 3
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample answers to unrelated questions after random-answer or true-answer fine-tuning.
rows.baseline: True-answer fine-tuned model answers shown in Table 1
rows.value: Random-answer fine-tuned model answers shown in Table 1; first three examples match the gold answer, fourth is incorrect
rows.note: Table presents examples rather than an aggregate error rate; it also includes a training example in its fifth example, which is excluded from this held-out result row.
rows.check: These examples concern unrelated factual answers and cannot establish V1's random-label test error. The extracted correctness count is wrong: the Apple-virus answer is correct; the ribs answer is incorrect. The displayed table contains six questions despite its caption numbering only five examples. These illustrative answers should not be treated as an aggregate error rate.

rows.subject: Lamini-1 MoME
rows.size_stated: massive mixture of memory experts; number not stated for this experiment
rows.stage_stated: pretrained transformer backbone augmented by adapters; backbone frozen during memory tuning
rows.operation_detail: Repeated randomization test, tuning selected memory experts on real or random answers.
rows.baseline: baseline Llama 3 result described as converging just as quickly
rows.note: MoME is an architecture changed from the standard network, so this result does not establish the unchanged-architecture clause of V1.
rows.check: Near-zero loss after 100 epochs is accurately reported, but MoME adds a purpose-built memory-expert architecture and selectively trains those experts. This does not test V1's standard-network, unchanged-architecture condition. Its comparison with baseline Llama 3 also differs from V2's real-label versus random-label comparison.
